questions.title: Why did the court treat prior instances of the sawed‑off rifle as “intrinsic” evidence rather than prohibited propensity evidence under Rule 404(b)?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the district court allowed D.F. and C.F. to testify that they had seen Cutbank with the sawed‑off Marlin .22 before the incident, calling it intrinsic evidence relevant to proving continuous possession. I thought evidence of prior conduct is generally barred as propensity under Rule 404(b) unless it falls under a recognized exception. How does the court justify treating these prior sightings as admissible, and what case law supports this distinction in the context of a firearms possession charge?

questions.title: What is the standard of review for a appellate court when deciding whether a district court’s failure to give a limiting instruction on hearsay violates the Confrontation Clause?
questions.question_body: Cutbank argued that the jury should have been instructed that D.F.’s statements to police were not substantive evidence until she testified, invoking the Confrontation Clause. The appellate panel cited United States v. Bennett and held that a later instruction is sufficient. What level of deference do appellate courts give to the trial judge’s discretion on such instructions, and are there any controlling precedents that require a limiting instruction at the time of admission rather than at the close of trial?

questions.title: How does the Eighth Circuit apply the "harmless error" doctrine to evidentiary mistakes in a firearms case?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeatedly references United States v. DeMarce and United States v. Keys, stating that the district court’s evidentiary rulings were not reversible because the error was harmless. Can someone explain the specific test the Eighth Circuit uses to determine harmlessness of evidentiary errors, especially when the error involves the admission of potentially prejudicial testimony about a victim’s family member’s death?

questions.title: What is the proper calculation of the sentencing guidelines range when multiple enhancements under §2K2.1(b)(6)(B) and the Armed Career Criminal Act overlap?
questions.question_body: The PSR gave Cutbank an offense level of 35, including a 4‑level enhancement for possession of a firearm in connection with another felony, plus other enhancements. The defense argues that this over‑counts because the ACCA already adds levels for similar conduct. How should a district court reconcile overlapping enhancements under the U.S.S.G. and ensure the correct “greater offense level” is applied per §4B1.4(b)?

questions.title: When is a district court required to provide a detailed recitation of the §3553(a) factors at sentencing?
questions.question_body: The appellate court noted that it is sufficient that the record shows the court considered the §3553(a) factors, citing United States v. Maluoth. However, I’m unclear on what constitutes an adequate showing. Does the district court have to explicitly list each factor and its analysis, or can a brief statement that the factors were considered satisfy the requirement? Are there any examples where a lack of detailed discussion led to reversal?

questions.title: Is extrinsic evidence of a witness’s prior inconsistent statement admissible for impeachment without the witness’s own testimony?
questions.question_body: In Cutbank’s case, the court refused to let the defense read portions of a police report to impeach C.F.’s testimony because the report wasn’t authored by C.F. The opinion cites United States v. Cumbie on authentication. Does the Eighth Circuit permit the use of written statements (e.g., police reports) to impeach a witness’s credibility if the witness does not testify to the content, and what are the authentication requirements?

questions.title: Does the presence of a sawed‑off firearm automatically trigger the §5845(a) firearm‑related offense level increase, or must the court find additional elements?
questions.question_body: The PSR applied a base offense level of 26 because the firearm was a sawed‑off rifle described in §5845(a). I’m trying to understand whether the mere possession of a sawed‑off weapon is sufficient for this enhancement, or if the court must also establish that the weapon was used in the commission of the crime. What is the controlling authority on this point in the Eighth Circuit?
